paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Universal basic income, a regular payment made to every citizen regardless of income or employment, has moved from the margins of economic debate to the centre of political discussion. Supporters, from technology entrepreneurs to social reformers, see it as a solution to poverty and a response to automation. Critics regard it as unaffordable and likely to discourage work. After reviewing the evidence, I conclude that it is neither the miracle its advocates claim nor the folly its opponents fear.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The strongest argument in its favour is simplicity. Existing welfare systems are often complicated, with conditions that trap people in poverty: a claimant who takes a part-time job may lose benefits and end up no better off. A universal payment removes this penalty, since everyone keeps it. It also avoids the stigma and administrative cost of means-testing, and reaches people who fail to claim benefits for which they are eligible.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Experiments provide some evidence. A trial in Finland in 2017 and 2018 gave two thousand unemployed people a monthly payment without conditions. Participants reported better wellbeing, less stress and greater trust in institutions, but the employment effect was small. Larger trials in Kenya, which gave payments to entire villages, found that recipients invested in small businesses and that local prices did not rise as sceptics feared. However, such trials are temporary and limited, and participants know the payments will end, so they may not predict how people would behave under a permanent national scheme.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Cost is the central objection. Paying every adult in a country like Britain a modest income would require hundreds of billions of pounds a year. This could be financed by higher taxes, by abolishing existing benefits or both, but then the question arises of who gains and who loses. A payment large enough to live on would require substantial tax rises; a smaller one might leave vulnerable groups, such as disabled people, worse off than before. Details determine whether the policy is progressive or not.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: My view is that the principle deserves experimentation, but that it should not be presented as a replacement for public services such as healthcare and education, which money alone cannot provide. A phased introduction, perhaps beginning with a partial payment, could test its effects while limiting risk. Whatever the outcome, the debate has performed a useful function: it has forced us to ask what we owe each other, and whether work is the only basis on which people deserve security.
